title: Fundraiser Challenge
goal: Your kid raises real money for a cause they care about. They find out who it helps and what a set amount buys, turn that into a goal they can picture, pick a way to raise it, ask people they know for support, count every dollar in the open, then give it and tell every donor exactly what their money did.
need: A cause your kid cares about, and a few minutes online with you to check it
A jar or tin with a label, and a notebook for every gift
What the fundraiser needs: baking supplies, buckets and sponges, or a route to walk
Paper and pencils for the goal chart

academics.subject: Math
academics.text: multiplying pledges and percent of a goal

academics.subject: Research
academics.text: finding who a cause helps and how

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: Your hardest job is staying quiet during the ask. Stand beside them when they talk to a neighbour, handle any money that comes in online, and let them explain the cause in their own words, even when it comes out shaky.

plan.what: Choose the cause and set the goal (Steps 1 and 2).
Make the asks, then raise and count (Steps 3 and 4).
Hand it over and send the report (Step 5).

troubleshoot.q: They picked a huge cause, like saving the ocean
troubleshoot.a: Find the local piece: a beach clean-up group or a wildlife rescue near you. Then ask what one amount buys there.
Report what they did reach, honestly: '3 bags of 4, 75%'. Donors care that the money went where it was promised more than that it hit the number.

troubleshoot.q: A relative offers to give the whole amount
troubleshoot.a: Thank them, and ask if they'd give last instead, as the gift that closes the gap. Your kid still does the asking, and the relative still helps.

lesson.text: Fundraising is asking people to give for something they'll never hold. They say yes when they can picture exactly what their money does, and they trust you next time when you come back and show them it did.
lesson.before: 'I'll put a jar out and see what happens.'

model.line: The local animal shelter. $30 buys one big bag of dog food.
$120, four bags, drawn on the fridge to colour in.
Bake sale $46, walk 8 sponsors × $1 a km × 9 km = $72. Total $118, 98%.
$2 of their own savings closed the gap. A photo of the four bags went to every donor.

lesson.modelNote: A jar with no cause or number asks people to guess. A named cost of $30 a bag gave every donor something to picture, and the photo of four real bags showed them it happened.

steps.title: Choose a cause and check it
steps.why: People give to a cause they can picture. Your kid has to picture it first.
steps.kid: Your kid lists three things they care about, like animals, a park clean-up group or kids in hospital, and picks one. Then they find out who it helps and what a set amount buys, using the Cause check card in the Fundraiser Toolkit at the end of the guide.
steps.you: Look the charity up together on your country's official charity list, or call a local group you know, like a shelter or food bank. Make any call or email yourself, and let them ask the question.
steps.tip: A local cause works best. Your kid can see the shelter, the clean-up or the food bank, and so can the people they ask.

levels.explore: Pick the cause, and draw who it helps.
levels.develop: Fill in the Cause check card, and find what $10 and $25 buy.
levels.extend: Compare two charities for the same cause, and decide which one your money would help more, and why.

steps.title: Set a goal you can picture
steps.why: 'Raise a lot' isn't a goal. 'Four bags of dog food' is.
steps.kid: Your kid turns what one amount buys into a goal, using the Goal math card, and draws it on a chart for the fridge as things to colour in. Then they pick a way to raise it from the Ways to raise card. For a sponsored challenge, they use the Sponsor math card to work out how far they'd need to go.
steps.you: Check the goal is reachable in a couple of weeks with the people you know. Smaller and reached beats big and half done.
ask: How many people would need to give to reach it?
Which way of raising fits you best?
steps.tip: For a bake sale or car wash, ask family to donate the supplies, so every dollar goes to the cause.

levels.explore: Choose how many things to give, like four bags, and draw them on the chart.
levels.develop: Work out the goal, pick a way to raise it, and estimate what it will bring in.
levels.extend: Ask a relative or a local business, with a parent, to match what you raise up to a set amount, and work out how much you now need to raise yourself.

steps.title: Make the ask
steps.why: Asking for money face to face is brave. A script makes it doable.
steps.kid: Your kid writes their ask using The ask card and practises it on you twice. Then they ask people they know: family, neighbours, friends' parents, a grandparent on a video call. For a sponsored challenge, each sponsor writes their pledge in the notebook.
steps.you: Stand beside them for every ask, or join the call. Ask only people you know. If anyone wants to give online, you handle it and write it in the notebook together.
ask: What did people ask you back?
steps.tip: Thank the people who say no, too. 'Thanks for listening' keeps every door open.

levels.explore: Say one sentence about your cause to a grandparent or neighbour, with a parent beside you.
levels.develop: Write the ask, practise it twice, and ask at least five people.
levels.extend: With a parent, ask a shop you already know to donate something you can use, like flour or a prize, and log what it's worth.

steps.title: Raise it and count it
steps.why: It's other people's money now. Counting it in the open is how they keep the trust.
steps.kid: Your kid runs the fundraiser: the bake sale, the car wash or the sponsored walk. Every gift goes in the notebook: who, how much and how. After every count, done by two people, they colour in the goal chart and work out the percent with the Goal math card. After a sponsored challenge, they go back to each sponsor with the final count, collect the pledge, and log it.
steps.you: Count with them every time, out loud. Keep the money somewhere safe, apart from family money.
ask: How far are you from the goal now?
Which part brought in the most?
steps.tip: Write 'anonymous' for a gift with no name. Every dollar still goes in the book.

levels.explore: Drop each gift in the jar, and colour in the chart with a parent.
levels.develop: Log every gift, count with a second person, and work out the percent of the goal.
levels.extend: If anything cost money, work out how many cents of every dollar given reached the cause, and why charities share that number.

steps.title: Give it and report back
steps.why: Donors gave without getting anything back. The report is what they get.
steps.kid: Your kid hands over the money, or sends it with you, and asks for a receipt or a photo of what it bought. Then they write a short report for every donor, using the Report back card: the total, where it went, what it did and a thank-you.
steps.you: Go with them to hand it over if you can. Send the report from your phone or email, or help them deliver notes by hand.
ask: What would you tell someone thinking of giving?
steps.tip: A photo of the real thing, like four bags stacked at the shelter, says more than the number.

levels.explore: Draw what the money bought, and give the drawing to one donor.
levels.develop: Write the report with all five parts, and send it to every donor.
levels.extend: Find out a month later what the cause needs next, and send donors a short second update.

skills.name: Asking
skills.text: speaking up for a cause with nothing to sell

skills.name: Following through
skills.text: coming back to say what the money did

conclusion.headline: They raised it, gave it and showed everyone what it did.
conclusion.text: Hand them the next donation box or sponsor form that comes your way, before you decide anything. Notice whether they ask what the money buys first.
conclusion.celebrate: When they give the report to the first donor, say: 'People trusted you with their money, and you showed them exactly where it went.'
extensions: Run the same fundraiser for the same cause a year later, and compare the totals
Visit a food bank or shelter and ask how they decide what to spend donations on
Start a family giving jar for the year, and vote together on where it goes
Read a real charity's yearly report together, and find what share went to the work itself

signs: They ask where the money goes before giving
They thank people who say no
They count other people's money carefully
makeItReal: At dinner this week, ask your kid what they'd raise money for if they could pick anything, and what $10 would buy there.

classroom.intro: A class fundraiser can raise real money for a real cause when it runs through the school. Students choose the cause, set a goal they can picture and run the event, while you and the office handle permission and the money.

tips.d: Before anything is announced, check with your principal or office about fundraising rules, how money is handled and which charities are allowed. Pick a cause the class can check on the official charity list.
Choose an event that fits school: a bake sale at recess if food rules allow, a used-book swap, or a class market day for other classes. Families can sponsor a class challenge too.
Split the class into cause checkers, goal math, ask writers, event crew and reporters. Each committee uses its own card from the Fundraiser Toolkit and reports to the class every session.
Every gift goes in the class notebook, and two people count out loud, with you as one of them. Money is locked away and handed to the office, never carried home by students.
Explore students colour the class chart after each count, Develop students work out the percent of the goal, and Extend students work out how many cents of each dollar reached the cause.
After giving day, the class writes one report for donors using the Report back card, sent home through your usual family channels. Celebrate what was reached, even if it's short of the goal.

classroom.timing: Plan about two weeks: one session to choose the cause and set the goal, two or three to plan the asks and the event, the event itself, then one session to count, give and report back. Asks to family happen at home.
